name: Ephrata Cloister AKA Ephrata Community
notes: Founded as a monastic religious community. Restructured as a both-gender community in 1814. Branches were established at other locations, of which two are said to still exist today.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Wisdom's Valley”.

name: Mount Lebanon Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Holy Mount”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “City of Peace”.

name: Canterbury Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Holy Ground”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Lovely Vineyard”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “City of Union”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “City of Love”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Holy Land”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Chosen Vale”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Pleasant Garden”.

notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Chosen Land”.

notes: A Harmonites village. The Harmony Society is a Christian theosophy and pietist society founded in Iptingen, Germany, in 1785.

name: Union Village Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Wisdom's Paradise”.

name: Watervliet Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Vale of Peace”.

name: South Union Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Jasper Valley”.

name: Gorham Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Union Branch”.

name: New Harmony, Indiana
notes: A Harmonites village. Colonists were formerly living in Harmony, Pennsylvania. Moved out to Old Economy Village. Sold the property to Robert Owen who himself founded a short-lived utopian settlement there.

name: Zoar
notes: Founded by German religious separatists who wanted religious freedom in America. Prosperous by the 1890s when it was one of the three strongest communistic societies in the U.S.

name: North Union Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Holy Grove”.

name: Whitewater Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Lonely Plain of Tribulation”.

name: Old Economy Village
notes: A Harmonites village. Colonists formerly lived in Harmony and New Harmony.

name: Nashoba Community
notes: "Emancipation Plantation" conceived by Miss Frances "Fanny" Wright.

name: New Harmony
notes: Former Harmonite village bought by British reformer Robert Owen. It then became a short-lived Owenite colony. Josiah Warren formed his anarchist beliefs from his experience there.

name: Yellow Springs Community
notes: Launched in July, terminated end of December 1825. Current home of Antioch College.

name: Blue Spring Community
located_by: Van Buren Township, Monroe County, Indiana
notes: About seven miles southwest of Bloomington.

name: Feiba Peveli
notes: Also known as "No. 3." Splinter group of English farmers from New Harmony, which survived the original colony's demise.

name: Kendal Community
notes: "Longest life of any Owenite Project." Voted to terminate January 3, 1829.

name: Macluria
notes: Also known as "No. 2." Splinter group of religious Westerners from New Harmony.

name: Sodus Bay Shaker Village
notes: A Fourierist community.

name: Wanborough Community
notes: Mentioned in Lockwood (1905) as having been established by May 1826.

name: New Philadelphia Colony
notes: A libertarian socialist community

name: United Order
notes: Based on the Law of Consecration, a revelation from Joseph Smith who was the founder of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints and Mormonism

name: Oberlin Colony
notes: Community based on Communal ownership of property

name: Community of United Christians at Berea, Ohio
notes: Intended to be an ideal Christian community (referred to as a lyceum village). The founders pooled their land and hoped to create a Utopian "Community of United Christians." Members of the Community vowed to avoid all luxuries and temptations that would prevent them from achieving the Methodist ideal of "sanctification," or perfect love of God. Baldwin later helped found Baldwin Wallace College.

name: Groveland Shaker Village
notes: Shaker spiritual name: “Union Branch”.

name: Brook Farm Institute of Agriculture and Education
notes: Unitarian Transcendentalist until 1844, Fourierist thereafter.

name: Hopedale Community
notes: A Fourierist community based on "Practical Christianity", which included ideas such as temperance, abolitionism, Women's rights, spiritualism and education.

name: Northampton Association
notes: Abolitionist community. Owned some 500 acres, a silk factory, and a sawmill. Workers did not get a wage but a profit share. (see Clark, Christopher, The Communitarian Moment: The Radical Challenge of the Northampton Association. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1995)

name: Social Reform Unity
notes: Later the Goose Pond Community

name: Sylvania Association
notes: Horace Greeley was Treasurer of this phalanx. Link to Sylvania Association webpage.

name: Fruitlands
notes: A Transcendent community.

name: Iowa Pioneer Phalanx
notes: Founded by members of the Jefferson County Industrial Association.

name: LaGrange Phalanx
notes: described in Ch. 8 & 9 of The Salt and the Savor, Howard W. Troyer, 1950.

name: McKean County Association
notes: Also known as “Teutonia.”

name: Moorehouse Union
notes: Straddled and crossed county line with Herkimer County.

name: North American Phalanx
notes: Last surviving Fourierist Association from the 1840s boom.

name: Prairie Home Community
notes: Also known as "Grand Prairie Community."

name: Skaneateles Community
notes: A Society for Universal Inquiry and Reform community, based on Fourierist principles at least at first.

name: Zanesfield Phalanx
notes: Also known as "Upper Domain" or "Highland Home." Small offshoot of Prairie Home Community, visited by MacDonald in August 1843.

name: Alphadelphia Association
notes: Fourierist community. Published commune's newspaper, The Alphadelphia Tocsin

name: Clarkson Industrial Association
notes: Also known as the “Western New York Industrial Association.”

name: Clermont Phalanx
notes: Established in aftermath of Sept. 1843 Pittsburgh "Western Fourier Convention."

name: Goose Pond Community
notes: Formerly the Social Reform Unity

name: Ohio Phalanx
notes: Established in aftermath of Sept. 1843 Pittsburgh "Western Fourier Convention."

name: Sodus Bay Phalanx
notes: A Fourierist community.

name: Trumbull Phalanx
notes: Established in aftermath of Sept. 1843 Pittsburgh "Western Fourier Convention."

name: Wisconsin Phalanx
notes: One of the longest-lived phalanxes of the 1840s boom.

name: Fruit Hills
notes: A community based on Owenism and anarchism. Maintained close contact with the Kristeen and Grand Prairie Communities.

name: Integral Phalanx
notes: Established in aftermath of Sept. 1843 Pittsburgh "Western Fourier Convention." Residents later moved to Illinois and established the Sangamon Phalanx.

name: Kristeen Community
notes: Founded by Charles Mowland and others who had previously been associated with the Prairie Home Community. A Society for Universal Inquiry and Reform community.

name: Sangamon Phalanx
notes: Continuation of the Integral Phalanx

name: Bishop Hill Colony
notes: A Swedish Pietist religious commune.

name: Spring Farm Association
notes: A Fourierist community.

name: Utopia
notes: Decentralized community based on equitable commerce or mutualism. replaced a Spiritualist community that in turn had replaced a Fourierist community.

name: Icarians Nauvoo, Icaria, etc.
place: Texas; Nauvoo, Illinois; Corning, Iowa; Cheltenham, Missouri; Cloverdale, California
notes: Egalitarian communities based on the French utopian movement founded by Cabet, after his followers emigrated to the US.

name: Oneida Community
notes: A religious Utopian socialist community. Oneida Community practices included Bible communism, Complex Marriage, Free love, Stirpiculture, Male Continence, Mutual Criticism and Ascending Fellowship. Other Noyesian communities were founded in Wallingford, Connecticut; Newark, New Jersey; Putney and Cambridge, Vermont.

name: Modern Times
notes: Founded upon individual sovereignty, equitable commerce and mutualism.

name: Aurora Colony
notes: Christian utopian community

name: Raritan Bay Union
notes: A Fourierist community.

name: Free Lovers at Davis House
notes: A community based on Free love and spiritualism.

name: Amana Colonies
notes: The Amana villages were built one hour apart when traveling by ox cart. Each village had a church, a farm, multi-family residences, workshops and communal kitchens. Operated woolen and flour mills. Prosperous by the 1890s when it was one of the three strongest communistic societies in the U.S. Its communal aspects narrowed in 1932, but its extensive holdings of farm and woodland never divided. Gave rise to the Amana Corporation, a maker of kitchen appliances.

name: La Réunion
notes: A Fourierist community.

name: Octagon City
notes: Originally built as a vegetarian colony north of the present-day site of Chanute, Kansas near Vegetarian Creek, a tributary of the Neosho River

name: Silkville
notes: Sericulture farm in Kansas that was founded on Fourierian principles. Later shifted away from Fourierism before its collapse.

name: Workingmen's Co-operative Colony
notes: A community based on the political reform philosophy of Chartist James Bronterre O'Brien.

name: Union Colony
notes: An agricultural temperance community bankrolled by Horace Greeley. Initiated by Nathan Meeker with an article in The New York Tribune in Nov 1869. Meeker selected 800 people from letters submitted and started the colony in May 1870. Still a thriving community but gradually moved away from the ideas of utopia and temperance.

name: Progressive Colony, near Cedar Vale
notes: A Russian communist colony with a mixture of atheism and liberal Christianity. Fell apart due to the domineering and sometimes cruel manner of its founder.

name: Zion Valley
notes: Bickertonite Mormon religious colony that secularized in 1879 to become the town of St. John, Kansas.

name: Danish Socialist Colony
notes: A utopian socialist community near Hays

name: Esperanza
notes: A utopian communist community founded by settlers from Missouri.

name: Rugby
notes: A community based on Christian socialism. “Associations” (joint-stock corporations) operated general store and other businesses. A tomato cannery and Rugby Pottery Company operated as joint-stock enterprise but failed financially. Hughes left scene in 1887, $250,000 poorer.

name: Am Olam
place: Oregon and various locations across the US
notes: Jewish social movement that sought to create agricultural communities in America.

name: Shalam Colony
notes: A community in which members would live peaceful, vegetarian lifestyles, and where orphaned urban children were to be raised.

name: Kaweah Colony
notes: Inspired by the scientific socialism of Laurence Gronlund and Edward Bellamy. Livelihood based on logging of giant sequoia trees. This ended with creation of the Sequoia National Park. "Squatter's Cabin" is last surviving structure of the colony.

name: Altruria
notes: Christian socialist colony inspired by William Dean Howells' 1884 novel A Traveler from Altruria.

name: Fairhope Single Tax Corporation, Fairhope, AL
notes: Fairhope was first settled in 1894 by Georgists. The Single tax experiment was incorporated as the Fairhope Single Tax Corporation under Alabama law in 1904. The municipality of Fairhope was incorporated in 1908.

name: Glennis Cooperative Industrial Colony
place: near Clear Lake, Puget Sound, Washington State
notes: Inspired by Bellamy's book, Looking Backward, 2000–1887. Established with the goal “own and operate manufactories, to acquire land, to build houses for its employees; to insure the employees against want, or the fear of want; and to maintain harmonious social relationships on the basis of cooperation.” started as farm, suffered agricultural problems and broke up. Part of the dissension was apparently from the persuasive anarchist teaching done by Tacoma tailor Andrew Klemencic. Glennis's founders tried again at the Home Colony, Key Peninsula.

name: Koreshan Unity
notes: Believed in Teed as a Messiah named Koresh, entered heavy decline after Teed's death in 1908.

name: Ruskin Colony
notes: Attempt to create a co-operative communal movement. Principles of the community were inspired by Edward Bellamy's utopian novel, Looking Backward (1886). Communal dining hall and laundry, housing, medical care, education, equality, and job security. success hampered by no clear business plan. Eventually some members forced sale of land and disbandment.

name: Harmony
notes: The existing community of Harmony attempted to become an ideal settlement based on "unselfish principles of co-operation and brotherly love" under its articles of incorporation. Settlers were required to accept socialism and be Caucasian of good moral character. Lacking new members outside of the county, the attempt was discontinued in 1899.

name: Home Colony
notes: An intentional community based on anarchist philosophy

name: Nucla
notes: Established following the Panic of 1893. Originally called Piñon.

name: Bellamy Cooperative Colony
place: Lincoln County, Oregon (on the Depai Creek 4 miles north of the county seat of Lincoln)
notes: Principles of the community were inspired by Edward Bellamy's utopian novel, Looking Backward (1886) and its sequel novel Equality (1897).

name: Equality Colony
notes: Principles of the community were inspired by Edward Bellamy's utopian novel, Looking Backward (1886) and its sequel novel Equality (1897). In 1905 colony was divided by arrival of Alexander Horr and other adherents of Theodor Hertzka’s "Freeland" concept. Wave of arsons effectively ended the social experiment.

name: Freedom
notes: The colony's economy was based on a Labor Exchange, designed to eliminate poverty and want, through the creation of a “soft” currency that served as legal tender. At the colony's warehouse, workers exchanged goods for “labor checks” redeemable for items in the warehouse.

name: Arden Village
notes: An art colony founded as a Georgist single-tax art community. Two nearby centres also ascribed to Georgist principles - Ardentown, founded in 1922, and Ardencroft, founded in 1950.

name: Freeland Association
notes: A socialist commune. The first settlers dissident members of the nearby Equality Colony. While the Freeland Association dissolved in 1906 the census-designated place (CDP) of Freeland, Washington continues to exist.

name: Zion, Illinois
notes: A Utopian Christian religious community, reorganized following fraud allegations and founder's death into modern city.

name: Helicon Home Colony
notes: A "co-operative home". A "home colony," in which to "secure the advantage of the application of machinery to domestic processes, and incidentally to solve the problem of the management of servants."

name: Free Acres
notes: Georgist community

name: Llano del Rio
notes: Project designed by architect and planner Alice Constance Austin with strong emphasis on shared domestic work

name: New Llano
notes: Founded by Job Harriman & other members of the California Llano del Rio colony who relocated to Louisiana.

name: Holy City
notes: Founded by a sect that promoted celibacy, temperance and a segregationist interpretation of Christianity.

name: Jersey Homesteads
notes: socialist Jewish farming community formed as part of F.D.R.'s New Deal. Its history is presented in a 1983 documentary Roosevelt, New Jersey: Visions of Utopia

name: Druid Heights
notes: Bohemian and artistic community. A meeting place used by three U.S. countercultural movements—the Beat Generation of the 1950s, the hippie movement of the 1960s, and the women's movement of the 1970s.

name: Kerista Commune
place: New York ("Old Tribe"); San Francisco ("New Tribe")
notes: Polyamorous new religious movement with communal ownership and a polyfidelitous nightly sleeping schedule.

name: Padanaram Settlement
notes: Christian fundamentalist commune in rural Indiana

name: Twin Oaks
notes: Originally a behaviourist utopian society based on the novel Walden Two; eventually becoming an egalitarian commune.

name: The Farm
notes: Buddhist-inspired Hippie vegetarian community. De-collectivized in 1983.

name: East Wind Community
notes: A secular and democratic community in which members hold all communities assets in common.

name: Uranian Phalanstery and the associated First New York Gnostic Lyceum Temple
place: Lower East Side of Manhattan, New York
notes: follows the "Practice of the Eightfold Way on the Path" and exercise "Creativity in Practice of the Path". Fourierist.

name: Acorn Community Farm
notes: egalitarian commune; branched off of Twin Oaks.
